newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Bundesbank seeks to calm German EMU debate.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Bundesbank seeks to calm German EMU debate.

text.p: The Bundesbank on Thursday moved to calm a fierce debate within Germany over European monetary union, saying the issue was being clouded by calls for exact numerical adherence to the Maastricht criteria.

Central bank president Hans Tietmeyer told a news conference that insistence on nations getting their budget deficit down to exactly three percent of their gross domestic product -- a key requirement for EMU -- was obscuring the more important task of achieving sustainable convergence and lasting fiscal discipline.
"It is not appropriate only to look at the zero discussion," Tietmeyer said. He was referring to calls that the three percent limit must be interpreted as 3.0 percent and not 3.1, 3.2 or higher.
"It is more important to look at sustainability which is a criterion of the (Maastricht) Treaty."
The Bundesbank's news conference came after its council held its annual out-of-town meeting which this year took place in this picturesque Bavarian town nestling in the foothills of the Alps.
Tietmeyer's remarks were an apparent shot across the bows of Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber, who has insisted that nations must not be allowed any scope to overshoot the three percent level.

Stoiber, who has spearheaded a campaign calling for the strictest possible interpretation of the EMU convergence criteria, was quoted this week as saying it would be better to delay the launch of the single currency, scheduled for 1999, than to risk having a soft euro.
Stoiber's campaign has struck a chord with the German public which is concerned that the euro may be softer than the mark.

His remarks cast fresh doubt on whether the euro will be launched punctually and this week contributed to pressure on the mark on the foreign exchange markets as investors opted for safe havens from euro uncertainty.
Tietmeyer noted that both houses of the federal parliament had as early as December 1992 stressed the need for nations to prove that their budgets and economic convergence were sustainable.
"Three is a very important point but it would be too short-sighted to just think of that level," Tietmeyer said.
The Maastricht Treaty allows a certain overshoot of the three percent level in special circumstances.

The debate about how strictly the criteria should be interpreted caused such friction within Chancellor's Helmut Kohl's ruling coalition that Kohl last week committed himself to hit the 3.0 percent level exactly.
Stoiber is a leading member of the Christian Social Union, the Bavarian sister party to Kohl's Christian Democrats.

Many independent economists doubt that Germany will be able to get its budget deficit down to 3.0 percent or lower but they, as well as a number of Bundesbank officials, have stressed that the Treaty allows leeway in interpretation.
France recently said that its deficit in 1997 will be much higher than 3.0 percent.
